tracks.title: Will it cross?
tracks.text: Lesson three point two — audits. This one is a sub-lesson, under toolkit. The parent lesson left you at what it called the honest frontier. Most software crosses into the sandbox cleanly… some puts up a fight. [curious] Fine. But which fight — yours? The audit is the instrument that answers that. A verdict, per dependency. Three words — ready… convertible… blocked. No build attempt. No vibes. And it writes the remaining work, as a checklist, into the toolkit itself. This lesson is the machinery underneath that frontier.

tracks.title: Will it cross?
tracks.text: First — will it cross? You have a tool that works. A skill with a few scripts… an MCP config… an npm CLI you reach for daily. You want it inside the sandbox, where it composes with everything else. Everywhere else, the way you find out if it will run is a shrug dressed as a workflow. Attempt the build… watch it break… read the wreckage… guess what to change… attempt again. [sighs] The feedback comes late, costs an engine, and arrives as a stack trace instead of a plan. And worse — it is per-build, not per-dependency. A red X on the whole thing tells you nothing about which of your six dependencies is the one that can't follow. What you actually want is two things. First… a verdict per dependency, assigned before you spend a single build. And second… the remaining work itemized — because the one doing the conversion is very likely an agent. And an agent needs a list, not a hunch.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. The audit is a static, offline classification of every carried script against the wasm lanes. Three verdicts — ready… convertible… blocked. Written into the toolkit's own manifest. With a checkbox fix-up plan for everything that isn't ready. The module that does the work states its creed in three words at the top of the file — static, offline, honest. Static… because it never runs your code. It reads it. Offline… because it needs no engine to render the report. And honest… because a diagnosis is not a failure. The bare audit always exits zero — even when every script is blocked. Telling you the truth is the success condition.

tracks.title: Stage two of three
tracks.text: [curious] The audit doesn't stand alone. It is the middle of a three-stage intake ramp — the path an existing tool walks to become a toolkit. Picture the flow as a line, left to right. On the left… an existing tool — a skill, an MCP server, an npm CLI. It enters stage one — import — which is parse-only. Import scaffolds a manifest, the skills, and the carried scripts… and then it leaves a piece of bait — a heading that reads, TODO dependency audit. Now the arrow. At the end of every import, automatically, the tool flows into stage two. The audit scans, classifies… and then write-into-manifest replaces that bait with a real section titled, dependency audit, static, auto. And in the very same pass, stage three writes the fix-up plan right below it — TODO fix-up plan, zero of n. There's one more arrow, dotted, looping back in — wbx toolkit audit, the directory. You can re-run it anytime… and every run replaces the last. The crucial detail — you never have to remember to audit. The moment a tool is scaffolded, it is diagnosed. And if the audit somehow errors, the import still succeeds and just prints, audit skipped. The spec's whole philosophy in one line — parse what's parseable, do the work, and leave a manual… never a shrug.

tracks.title: Three words
tracks.text: Three words. Every dependency reduces to one of three classes — and each verdict is a commitment, not a mood. Ready… the lane covers it today. Push it, it runs. Convertible… a known recipe exists, but it needs work — a build, a shim, a re-route. The crossing is real but charted. And blocked… native-only. It needs a redesign, or an engine-side capability with no sandbox equivalent. Now, the verdicts come from two fixed truth tables — one for interpreters, read from the shebang… and one for binaries, spotted at command position. Let me read you the ones that matter. Shell — bash, zsh, plain sh — ready. The posix shape runs in the sandbox. Node and JavaScript — ready — that's the quickjs lane, most of Node's surface. Python, ruby, and perl — blocked. No lane today. The tool jq — ready — it compiles to wasm cleanly through the C lane. The tool ffmpeg — also ready — but for a lovely reason. It is already a shipped toolkit, so you depend on it instead of bundling it. Then the convertibles. Curl and wget — convertible — network is engine-brokered, so route through the Dock, not raw sockets. Git — convertible — call the engine-side git, not a local binary. And the npm family — convertible — resolve and bundle at build time, not install at runtime. And the blocked ones — docker, sudo, the host package managers like brew and apt, the desktop hooks like osascript. All blocked — they have no sandbox meaning. [curious] One sharp thing — node shows up twice on purpose. As an interpreter it is ready, because you're running JavaScript. As a binary you shell out to… it is convertible, because that's install-at-runtime, which the npm lane wants to replace. The audit judges the role — not just the name.

tracks.title: How it looks without running
tracks.text: Now a depth rung — how it looks without running. You can skip this one. Static means the audit reads text and reasons about it — it never executes it. It's a stack of small, honest heuristics. First… the interpreter, from the shebang. The hash-bang line names it… and env-node is handled by taking the token after the word env. No shebang? Fall back to the file extension. Second… binaries, at command position. A shell-ish heuristic that's good enough offline — each line is split on the shell operators, the first word of each segment is taken as a command, a leading dollar sign is stripped, and the set is deduped. Comment lines are skipped. Third… npm dependencies, by sniffing the require and from lines for their package names. And fourth… pip dependencies — but only under python — where import lines become blocked findings. [curious] And here's the most important line in the whole scanner — the line about what it does not say. The binary list is deliberately short. Every binary it doesn't recognize returns nothing — unremarkable or unknown… don't speculate. The audit stays silent about tools it doesn't know, on purpose. Silence is not endorsement. It's the refusal to invent a verdict it can't defend.

tracks.title: Worst-of wins
tracks.text: Worst-of wins. A script usually has more than one dependency… so the audit needs a rule for rolling its findings into one verdict. The rule is severity, worst-of. Ready is zero. Convertible is one. Blocked is two. A script's class is the maximum severity of any finding inside it. The consequence is bracing, and correct — one finding poisons the whole script. A hundred clean lines of bash… and a single import numpy… and the verdict is blocked. Because that one line is what will stop it crossing — and an audit that averaged it away would be lying to you. Picture a real script — fetch dot sh — with two findings. The bash interpreter… ready, severity zero. The curl binary… convertible, severity one. Take the worst of the two, and fetch dot sh rolls up to convertible. The shell itself was fine. The curl is the part that needs a re-route. So convertible is the honest verdict — the worst of what's inside, surfaced as the verdict of the whole.

tracks.title: The artifact carries its own audit
tracks.text: Here is the move that makes this more than a linter — the artifact carries its own audit. The findings don't go to a log you'll close. They go into the toolkit's own manifest. The audit finds the stage-one heading — TODO dependency audit — truncates from there, and appends a fresh section. It is idempotent by design — every run replaces the last, so the carried audit can never go stale. This is the parent lesson's whole thesis — the manual is the interface — recursed one level down. A verdict that lives in the artifact… can't disagree with the artifact. Let me read you the before and after. Before — stage one leaves bait. The heading reads, TODO dependency audit. And underneath, a note — the import was parse-only… next, the wasm compatibility audit classifies every carried script and writes the fix-up plan here. After the audit runs… that heading is gone. In its place — a section titled, dependency audit, static, auto. Then a sub-heading — calc dot py, blocked, python3. And two finding lines beneath it. One — interpreter python3, blocked, no python lane today. Two — pip numpy, blocked, no python lane. [curious] And the empty case is just as honest. A toolkit with no scripts directory — pure guidance, manuals only — gets a one-line section that says exactly that. No carried scripts… guidance-only toolkit… nothing to convert. The audit never pads. And it never pretends there's work where there isn't.

tracks.title: The agent manual
tracks.text: The agent manual. The findings tell you what can't cross. Stage three — the fix-up plan, written in the same pass — tells you what to do about it, in a grammar an agent already executes. Only the non-ready scripts become work. A fully-ready toolkit gets a short, honest line — nothing to fix, every script is sandbox-ready. Otherwise, the plan opens with a real org checkbox cookie — TODO fix-up plan… zero of n… where n is the count of non-ready scripts. Let me read you the plan for that blocked python script. The heading — TODO fix-up plan, zero of three. Then a preamble — the agent manual… work each item, check it off, then prove the whole toolkit, done when push, build, and verify all pass. Then a sub-heading — TODO calc dot py, blocked, python3. And four checkboxes, each an open box. First — rewrite in JavaScript for the quickjs lane… keep the script's CLI contract, same args in, same stdout out, so callers don't change. Second — or split the logic into org tasks the engine runs natively. Third — numpy goes away with the python rewrite. And fourth — re-run the audit… calc dot py must classify ready. [excited] Two things are doing the real work. The zero-of-three cookie is a live progress meter — work items, check them, watch the fraction climb. And the final checkbox is the masterstroke — the done-test for converting the script is re-running the very tool that judged it. The plan is machine-checkable… because its acceptance criterion is another run of the audit.

tracks.title: Closing the loop
tracks.text: Closing the loop. The bare audit diagnoses. Add the fix flag… and it converts — by running the exact three commands the plan named, against a live engine. Push… build… verify. Picture it as a conversation between two participants — your machine running wbx, and the engine. First, wbx talks to itself — scan, classify, write the manifest. Then, if the fix flag is set and an engine is reachable… wbx sends the zipped toolkit to install. The engine replies — pushed. wbx asks for a build. The engine replies — built. wbx asks to verify. The engine replies — verified. And wbx exits zero, printing, fix… pushed… built… verified. But if the fix flag is set and no engine answers… the install call comes back unreachable, and wbx exits three — with a hint to start one with wbx deploy local. That three is the key. The bare audit on a broken setup still exits zero — a diagnosis isn't a failure. But fix with no engine exits three. And three is part of a fixed exit-code map every wbx verb shares, so agents can branch on it. Zero means ok — read the report, work the plan. Three means engine unreachable — start one, retry. Four means not found — fix the path. Five means verification failed — the conversion is wrong, re-open the plan. And one honest note — the engine-side verify is structural. Manifest present, skills present, trust checks. It even reports that native bash blocks are disabled, by the platform's native-exec ban. Verify confirms the toolkit is well-formed and compatible. It does not confirm it is correct. That's a different gate.

tracks.title: What the audit will not tell you
tracks.text: Now the honest part — what the audit will not tell you. The audit is sharp precisely because it knows its edges. First… the scope is the scripts directory only. It reads the files directly in that one folder — non-recursive, nothing else. A toolkit with no scripts directory gets an empty audit. The spec gestures at scanning for network and filesystem expectations… but today's code doesn't do that, and this lesson sides with the code. Second… the parse is heuristic, not a real shell parser. Good enough offline — it reads the common shapes well, but it won't catch every exotic construction. Third… silence is not a blessing. A binary it doesn't flag isn't certified safe — it's unrecognized, and the audit refuses to speculate. Fourth… blocked means no lane today. The python verdict is dated, not eternal — the day a python lane ships, that verdict changes. And fifth… compatibility is not correctness. Ready means it'll run in the sandbox — not that it does the right thing. A script can be perfectly ready and perfectly wrong. Verify is structural. Evals are the separate gate for whether the behavior is any good.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Why did my manifest change after import? Because the audit auto-runs at the end of every import and writes its findings straight into the manifest — that's the design. It replaced the placeholder with the real report and the plan. Re-running replaces it again, so it never goes stale. It said ready — why did the build still fail? Because ready is a static verdict about lane coverage, not a build attempt. The node verdict says it plainly — quickjs covers most of Node's surface… but full-Node APIs may need shims. Python is blocked — forever? No. Blocked means no lane today. It reflects the lanes that currently exist… not a permanent judgment. It didn't flag a weird binary I use — am I safe? Not necessarily — you're unjudged. Silence means no verdict, not approved. Do I need an engine to audit? No. The bare audit is fully static and offline — it scans, classifies, writes the manifest, and exits zero. You only need an engine for the fix flag. And — what does an agent do with the plan? [chuckles] It works it like any other plan. The checkboxes are plain org grammar — it does each recipe step, checks it off, re-runs the audit to confirm, and proves the whole toolkit with push, build, verify.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's the audit. Not a vibe about whether your tool will cross — a verdict, per dependency, assigned offline in milliseconds, with the reason attached… and the remaining work written as a checklist into the toolkit itself. A diagnosis isn't a failure. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under toolkit — lesson three — where the honest frontier was first drawn. Go read the parent for the bigger picture… or follow the ramp sideways to imports, which hands the audit its input, and to lanes, which every verdict is measured against. The audit is just the frontier… instrumented.
